annotator: Claude (Opus 5.5). Annotator A labelled all 745 reports; annotator B labelled, on its own, the 253 reports of 2026-08-12 to 2026-08-31 and 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-29. Both read only the title, the publisher, the UTC time and the first 700 characters of the text (URLs shown as [link]); no embeddings, no detector output and no events of the reader app. On the 253 reports the annotators agreed with MUC F1 0.991, B-cubed F1 0.997, CEAF-e F1 0.997 and CoNLL F1 0.995; 6 reports had an event with different members, all from one disagreement (r618, an Engadget live blog of the Apple event), which the adjudicator settled for annotator B by rules 5, 8 and 10. The other labels are those of annotator A.
boundaryRule:
1. One event is one announced action: a model or product launch, a deal or investment, a funding round or filing,
   a statement, a policy or report release, a lawsuit filing or ruling, a hire or departure, an incident disclosure.
2. A report about the reaction to an action (analysis, criticism, follow-up quotes, market moves), published within
   7 days after the action, belongs to that action. Published later than 7 days, it gets its own label.
3. A general feature, interview, opinion or round-up with no single action gets its own label (a singleton).
4. Two actions announced together in one post (one announcement) are one event. Two actions announced separately,
   even on one day and one topic, are two events.
5. When a report covers several actions, it gets the action of its title; if its title names none, the action of its
   lead. If it still has no single action, rule 3.
6. A later step in one case (a ruling after a filing, an appeal after a ruling) is a new action, so a new event.
7. Labels come from the title and the start of the text only, without embeddings or detector output. Unclear cases
   go to the ambiguous list with the alternative label.
8. A report about a scheduled or announced action, published in the 7 days before it, belongs to that action.
9. A media report of a deal or plan before the company announces it is its own event. The company's announcement is
   a separate event.
10. At a keynote, each separate announcement post is its own event (rule 4). A live blog, recap or opinion piece whose
   title names no single action is a singleton (rule 3). There is no event for the keynote as a whole. A recap whose
   title names one or more actions gets the first action of its title (rule 5).
11. A round-up or podcast whose title names one action gets that action (rule 5). Otherwise it is a singleton (rule 3).
12. Remarks made at one appearance (one interview, one press Q&A, one summit session) are one statement event.
   Remarks at separate appearances are separate events.
13. The 7 days are counted in UTC calendar dates, as the detector's window counts them. A reaction whose UTC date is
   at most 7 days after the UTC date of the action belongs to the action. A later reaction gets its own label.
14. A piece published more than 7 days later that repeats an earlier claim is its own event.
15. A recurring weekly post whose headline is a feature that another publisher reported in the 7 days before it
   belongs to the event of that report.
16. Two pages with the same title on one day are judged like any two reports.
17. A partner's post that serves, hosts, ships or supports another company's launch, published on the UTC date of the launch
   or the next UTC date, belongs to that launch: it reports the launch. A model's availability on a further platform that is
   announced separately on a later date is its own event (rule 4).
18. Tutorials, how-to guides, explainers, customer stories, case studies, benchmark comparisons, webinar recaps and the parts
   of a series are singletons (rule 3), unless the title or lead ties the post to one action of the 7 days before it (rule 2),
   for example a guide to a product that was launched that week.
19. Ignore banners, promotions, navigation, cookie notes and audio-player widgets that a site repeats at the top of its pages.
   Judge each report by its own title and its own text.

source.name: The reports of the reader app 'What is going on' (zukhruf #3142, #3205): the feeds and blogs of 41 AI labs and tech outlets, as the app had them on 2026-10-29
source.licence: The articles belong to their publishers. This repository holds only their URLs, dates, publishers and our labels. The app read each page with the user agent WhatIsGoingOn and followed the robots.txt of each site for that agent.
source.attribution: Articles by the 40 publisher hosts of answer-key.json. Labels by the zukhruf project.

weaknesses: The annotators and the adjudicator are AI models (Claude), not people. A second annotator labelled 253 of the 745 reports only.
The annotators read the title and the first 700 characters of the text, not the whole article.
32 reports are ambiguous; each has its alternative label.

The dates are those the app gave: the declared date of the page, else the feed date, else a date the page shows near its title. Some feeds give 12:00 UTC or 00:00 UTC for every post (ElevenLabs, Liquid AI).
The set leaves out the 50 reports that had no date in the app, and the 34 reports that anthropic-outlets (17) and deepmind-outlets (17) hold. It holds no report of nvidia-outlets.
Most outlets give only their last 20 feed items, so the outlet reports cover 2026-10-20 to 2026-10-29, and many lab reports from 2023 to 2026 have no outlet report. Most events have one report.

The texts are the textContent of elt's article extraction in the app's articles.sqlite of 2026-10-29 (the main database file, without its write-ahead log). They live only in the gitignored eval cache (cache/texts/labs-outlets.json), as the other web sets keep them (#3213). A text that the runner fetches again is extracted with Readability, so it can differ.
